title: Data Governance Maturity Diagnostic
description: 55 weighted questions across eleven DAMA-DMBOK / DCAM aligned pillars. 33 core questions form the sector-neutral chassis; 22 banking-overlay questions add regulatory and core-banking specificity. Scored 1–5 against anchored level descriptions, weighted 1–3 by decisiveness.

questions.text: Is there a named executive sponsor for data governance who controls budget and can influence the objectives of data owners?

levelDescriptions.1: No sponsor. Data governance is raised occasionally by individuals with no mandate.
levelDescriptions.2: A sponsor is named but holds influence only — no budget authority and no leverage over other departments.
levelDescriptions.3: A sponsor with budget authority is formally appointed and the appointment is documented.
levelDescriptions.4: The sponsor actively reallocates budget for data work and holds owners accountable in performance reviews.
levelDescriptions.5: Data accountability is embedded in executive objectives across the leadership team, not just the sponsor's.

questions.text: Are Data Owners formally named for each major domain, with accountability accepted in writing?

levelDescriptions.1: No ownership exists. Disputes about data are unresolvable or escalate to the chief executive.
levelDescriptions.2: Informal ownership is assumed for some systems, usually by whoever built or maintains them.
levelDescriptions.3: Data Owners are named per domain at department-head level and the accountability is documented.
levelDescriptions.4: Owners actively approve definitions, thresholds and access, and are measured on their domain's quality.
levelDescriptions.5: Ownership is a standing element of the role, transfers cleanly on personnel change, and is audited.

questions.text: Does a governance forum exist with the authority to make binding decisions on data definitions, standards and exceptions?

levelDescriptions.1: No forum exists. Data decisions are made unilaterally within each system or project.
levelDescriptions.2: A working group meets irregularly to share information but holds no decision rights.
levelDescriptions.3: A council is constituted with documented terms of reference, membership and quorum.
levelDescriptions.4: The council meets on cadence, records decisions, enforces quorum and tracks actions to closure.
levelDescriptions.5: The council is embedded in the corporate committee hierarchy and its decisions are treated as binding across the organisation.

questions.text: Is data governance connected into the bank's existing committee structure — risk, audit or ALCO — rather than operating in parallel to it?

levelDescriptions.1: No connection. Data governance, where it exists, is a technology initiative invisible to bank governance.
levelDescriptions.2: Occasional reporting into a technology committee; no risk or board-level visibility.
levelDescriptions.3: A defined reporting line into an established bank committee exists and is documented.
levelDescriptions.4: Data matters appear as standing agenda items with recorded decisions at a risk or board committee.
levelDescriptions.5: Data risk is a recognised risk category with defined appetite, reported to the board like any other risk.

questions.text: Have internal audit or regulatory examinations raised findings on data ownership, governance or accountability, and have those findings been closed durably?

levelDescriptions.1: Findings are open, repeat across cycles, or the area has never been examined.
levelDescriptions.2: Findings have been closed with documentation but no structural change; recurrence is likely.
levelDescriptions.3: Findings are tracked with owners and remediation plans that address root cause.
levelDescriptions.4: Structural remediation is evidenced and no repeat findings have arisen in the most recent cycle.
levelDescriptions.5: The bank self-identifies governance gaps ahead of examination and presents remediation proactively.

questions.text: Does a documented data strategy exist that is explicitly linked to funded business outcomes?

levelDescriptions.1: No data strategy. Data work is generated project by project with no connecting logic.
levelDescriptions.2: A strategy document exists but is generic, unfunded and disconnected from business plans.
levelDescriptions.3: The strategy is approved and maps initiatives to named business outcomes.
levelDescriptions.4: The strategy drives budget allocation and its progress is reviewed against outcome measures.
levelDescriptions.5: Data strategy is a component of corporate strategy, refreshed on the same cycle and tracked with the same rigour.

questions.text: Can the organisation quantify what poor data quality costs it — rework hours, reconciliation effort, duplicated pipelines or findings?

levelDescriptions.1: No quantification exists. The cost is acknowledged anecdotally but never measured.
levelDescriptions.2: Isolated estimates exist for individual incidents, produced reactively.
levelDescriptions.3: A cost-of-poor-data model exists covering the main categories with a documented method.
levelDescriptions.4: The cost is baselined, attributed to owning domains, and tracked over time.
levelDescriptions.5: Cost movement is attributed to specific governance interventions and used to prioritise investment.

questions.text: Is there a benefit baseline captured before governance work starts, against which improvement can be demonstrated?

levelDescriptions.1: No baseline. Success is described qualitatively or in terms of artefacts produced.
levelDescriptions.2: Baselines are reconstructed after the fact when someone asks for evidence of value.
levelDescriptions.3: Baselines are captured before work begins for the primary claimed benefits.
levelDescriptions.4: Baselines are measured on a defined cadence and variance is explained.
levelDescriptions.5: Benefit tracking is automated from operational systems and reported alongside financial results.

questions.text: Is the volume of rework in regulatory submissions — resubmissions, late corrections, manual adjustments — measured?

levelDescriptions.1: Not measured. Rework is absorbed into month-end effort and never surfaces as a metric.
levelDescriptions.2: Major resubmissions are remembered but no systematic record is kept.
levelDescriptions.3: Resubmissions, corrections and manual adjustments are logged per submission cycle.
levelDescriptions.4: Rework is trended, root-caused to specific data defects and attributed to owning domains.
levelDescriptions.5: Rework is near-zero by design, with pre-submission validation catching defects at source.

questions.text: Has the bank assessed which AI or advanced analytics use cases are blocked specifically by data readiness rather than by technology or funding?

levelDescriptions.1: No assessment. AI ambition and data reality have never been compared.
levelDescriptions.2: Anecdotal awareness that data is a problem, with no use-case-level analysis.
levelDescriptions.3: A documented readiness assessment exists per candidate use case.
levelDescriptions.4: Readiness gaps are costed, owned and sequenced into the data roadmap.
levelDescriptions.5: A data-readiness gate is embedded in the AI intake process; use cases cannot proceed without passing it.

questions.text: Is a system of record formally designated for each major subject area, and honoured by consuming systems?

levelDescriptions.1: No designation. Consumers pull from whichever source is most convenient.
levelDescriptions.2: Informal convention exists for some subject areas but is not documented or enforced.
levelDescriptions.3: Systems of record are designated and documented for the major subject areas.
levelDescriptions.4: Designation is enforced at the architecture-approval gate and deviations require exception approval.
levelDescriptions.5: Consumption is automatically traceable to designated sources and unauthorised sourcing is detected.

questions.text: Does a canonical logical data model exist for the governed domains, used as the reference for new development?

levelDescriptions.1: No enterprise model. Each system defines its own structures independently.
levelDescriptions.2: Models exist for individual systems but are not reconciled to each other.
levelDescriptions.3: A canonical logical model covers the governed domains and is published.
levelDescriptions.4: New development is assessed against the canonical model at design review.
levelDescriptions.5: The model is maintained as a living asset with change control, and physical implementations are traceable to it.

questions.text: Is the extent of duplicated data pipelines and redundant data copies known and managed?

levelDescriptions.1: Unknown. New extracts are created freely with no visibility of existing ones.
levelDescriptions.2: Suspected duplication is discussed but never inventoried.
levelDescriptions.3: An inventory of pipelines and copies exists and is periodically refreshed.
levelDescriptions.4: Duplication is measured, attributed to cost, and a retirement backlog is actively worked.
levelDescriptions.5: New pipeline creation requires justification against the existing inventory; duplication trends down.

questions.text: Are core banking structures — customer, arrangement, product, transaction — mapped to an industry banking reference model?

levelDescriptions.1: No mapping exists; no industry reference model is in use.
levelDescriptions.2: A reference model was acquired but the mapping was never completed or maintained.
levelDescriptions.3: Core subject areas are mapped to a banking reference model and the mapping is documented.
levelDescriptions.4: The mapping is maintained through change and used in impact analysis for new products.
levelDescriptions.5: The reference model drives design; product extensions are registered as governed gap extensions.

questions.text: Can risk and finance data be aggregated across systems to group level with demonstrable completeness and within required timeframes?

levelDescriptions.1: Aggregation is manual, slow and its completeness cannot be evidenced.
levelDescriptions.2: Aggregation works for routine reporting but breaks under ad hoc or stress-scenario demands.
levelDescriptions.3: Documented aggregation processes exist with defined completeness checks.
levelDescriptions.4: Aggregation is automated, completeness is evidenced, and timeframes are met consistently.
levelDescriptions.5: On-demand aggregation is available, including under stress conditions, with automated completeness assurance.

questions.text: Does an approved business glossary exist, with a single agreed definition for each key term?

levelDescriptions.1: No glossary. The same term carries different meanings in different departments without anyone reconciling them.
levelDescriptions.2: Departmental glossaries or spreadsheets exist and contradict each other.
levelDescriptions.3: An enterprise glossary exists with approved definitions for key terms and a defined approval route.
levelDescriptions.4: Definitions are maintained under change control, disputes are arbitrated by the council, and coverage is measured.
levelDescriptions.5: Glossary terms are bound to physical assets and surfaced in reporting and analytics tools at the point of use.

questions.text: Is technical metadata harvested automatically into a catalogue, rather than maintained manually?

levelDescriptions.1: No catalogue. Metadata exists only in system documentation and individual knowledge.
levelDescriptions.2: A catalogue exists but is populated manually and is significantly out of date.
levelDescriptions.3: Automated harvesting is configured for the main source systems on a defined schedule.
levelDescriptions.4: Coverage and freshness are measured, and harvest failures are alerted and resolved.
levelDescriptions.5: Harvesting spans the estate including pipelines and reporting layers, with near-real-time freshness.

questions.text: Are business terms bound to the specific physical columns that implement them?

levelDescriptions.1: No binding. The glossary, where it exists, is disconnected from any physical implementation.
levelDescriptions.2: Binding is described narratively in documents rather than recorded as structured links.
levelDescriptions.3: Governed terms are bound to their physical assets in the catalogue.
levelDescriptions.4: Binding coverage is measured against the CDE register and gaps are worked.
levelDescriptions.5: Binding is validated automatically and breaks when schemas change, triggering steward review.

questions.text: Where a regulator defines a term, is that definition authoritative in the glossary and reconciled against internal management definitions?

levelDescriptions.1: No distinction is drawn between regulatory and management definitions.
levelDescriptions.2: The difference is known informally and handled by individuals during report preparation.
levelDescriptions.3: Regulatory definitions are recorded as authoritative and management variants are documented separately.
levelDescriptions.4: Reconciliation between regulatory and management figures is documented and explained systematically.
levelDescriptions.5: Both variants are derived from the same governed source with the difference computed and explained automatically.

questions.text: Are product hierarchies — including Islamic banking variants where applicable — governed with a single approved structure?

levelDescriptions.1: Product structures differ across core banking, finance and reporting with no reconciliation.
levelDescriptions.2: A mapping exists between structures but is maintained manually and drifts.
levelDescriptions.3: A governed product hierarchy is approved with a defined change process.
levelDescriptions.4: All consuming systems derive from the governed hierarchy and drift is detected.
levelDescriptions.5: New product introduction requires governed hierarchy registration before it can be launched.

questions.text: Are executable data quality rules defined and running on a schedule against critical data elements?

levelDescriptions.1: No rules. Quality problems are discovered by the recipient of a report, after publication.
levelDescriptions.2: Ad hoc validation exists inside individual ETL jobs, undocumented and inconsistently applied.
levelDescriptions.3: A rule set is defined against critical elements and executes on a defined schedule.
levelDescriptions.4: Rules cover all governed CDEs, have owners and thresholds, and failures raise issues automatically.
levelDescriptions.5: Rules are version-controlled, tested, and enforced in pipelines so defective data is blocked rather than reported.

questions.text: Is a data quality scorecard published to business stakeholders on a regular cadence?

levelDescriptions.1: No scorecard. Quality is not reported in any structured form.
levelDescriptions.2: Quality metrics are produced sporadically, usually in response to an incident.
levelDescriptions.3: A scorecard is published on cadence covering the governed elements.
levelDescriptions.4: The scorecard has a named owner per failing measure, is reviewed at council, and trends are tracked.
levelDescriptions.5: The scorecard drives accountability — persistent failures affect owner objectives and funding decisions.

questions.text: Is there an issue management workflow with severity, ownership, SLA and root-cause analysis?

levelDescriptions.1: Issues are raised by email or in meetings and tracked in individuals' heads.
levelDescriptions.2: A spreadsheet or ticket queue exists but lacks severity, SLA or root-cause discipline.
levelDescriptions.3: A defined workflow exists with severity classification, ownership and target resolution times.
levelDescriptions.4: SLA adherence is measured, root cause is recorded, and recurring causes are escalated.
levelDescriptions.5: Root-cause remediation is funded and tracked, and recurrence rates measurably decline.

questions.text: Are reconciliation controls between general ledger, subledger and source systems automated and monitored?

levelDescriptions.1: Reconciliation is entirely manual, performed in spreadsheets at period end.
levelDescriptions.2: Partially automated for major accounts; breaks are investigated reactively with no trend analysis.
levelDescriptions.3: Automated reconciliation covers the main flows with documented tolerances and break handling.
levelDescriptions.4: Breaks are trended, aged, root-caused and attributed to owning domains.
levelDescriptions.5: Reconciliation runs continuously rather than at period end, and break volumes trend structurally down.

questions.text: Are the data inputs to provisioning and credit risk models subject to quality controls before the models consume them?

levelDescriptions.1: No input controls. Model outputs are challenged after the fact when results look implausible.
levelDescriptions.2: Modellers perform their own informal sanity checks with no standard or record.
levelDescriptions.3: Defined input quality checks exist and run before model execution.
levelDescriptions.4: Input quality is reported alongside model output and failures block model runs.
levelDescriptions.5: Output variance can be attributed between genuine credit movement and input data quality change.

questions.text: Is a single trusted version of the primary master entity — customer or party — defined and published to consuming systems?

levelDescriptions.1: Each system maintains its own version with no reconciliation between them.
levelDescriptions.2: A preferred source is nominated informally but consumers still use local copies.
levelDescriptions.3: A golden record is defined with documented survivorship rules and published.
levelDescriptions.4: Consuming systems subscribe to the golden record and local variants are being retired.
levelDescriptions.5: The golden record is authoritative estate-wide, with match confidence measured and exceptions stewarded.

questions.text: Is the duplicate rate within master entities measured and actively reduced?

levelDescriptions.1: Duplication is known to exist but has never been measured.
levelDescriptions.2: Ad hoc de-duplication exercises are run occasionally, usually before a campaign or audit.
levelDescriptions.3: Duplicate rate is measured on a defined method and reported.
levelDescriptions.4: A stewardship queue processes match exceptions continuously and the rate trends down.
levelDescriptions.5: Prevention controls at the point of creation keep new duplication near zero.

questions.text: Are reference data code sets registered with named owners and a controlled change process?

levelDescriptions.1: Code sets are embedded in applications and changed without notice or coordination.
levelDescriptions.2: Some code sets are documented; changes are communicated informally when remembered.
levelDescriptions.3: A register exists with owners and a defined change process.
levelDescriptions.4: Changes follow the process, are versioned, and downstream impact is assessed before release.
levelDescriptions.5: Code sets are distributed from a single governed service and drift is impossible by design.

questions.text: Can the bank reliably produce a single customer view for exposure aggregation, including related-party and group linkage?

levelDescriptions.1: No single customer view. Exposure aggregation is manual and its completeness cannot be evidenced.
levelDescriptions.2: A partial view exists for retail or for a single system, with known gaps.
levelDescriptions.3: A single customer view is defined and maintained across the main systems.
levelDescriptions.4: Group and related-party linkages are maintained and used in limit monitoring.
levelDescriptions.5: Aggregation is on demand with evidenced completeness, including indirect and connected exposures.

questions.text: Are national identifiers — CNIC, NTN or equivalent — validated at capture and used consistently as matching keys?

levelDescriptions.1: Identifiers are captured inconsistently, with format errors and placeholder values present.
levelDescriptions.2: Format validation exists in some channels but not others; historical data is unremediated.
levelDescriptions.3: Validation is applied at capture across channels and format rules are documented.
levelDescriptions.4: Historical records are remediated and identifier quality is measured on the scorecard.
levelDescriptions.5: Identifiers are verified against an authoritative external source and used as the primary matching key.

questions.text: Can lineage be traced from a published figure back to its source fields without a manual investigation?

levelDescriptions.1: No lineage. Tracing a figure requires interviewing whoever wrote the extract, and can take weeks.
levelDescriptions.2: Lineage exists as narrative documentation for some flows, of uncertain currency.
levelDescriptions.3: Lineage is captured in structured form for the governed elements.
levelDescriptions.4: Lineage is maintained automatically from pipeline execution and coverage is measured.
levelDescriptions.5: Lineage is complete end to end including reporting and analytics layers, and is used routinely in impact analysis.

questions.text: Is impact analysis performed using lineage before changes are made to data structures or pipelines?

levelDescriptions.1: No impact analysis. Downstream breakage is discovered by consumers after release.
levelDescriptions.2: Impact is assessed from memory and personal knowledge of the estate.
levelDescriptions.3: Lineage-based impact analysis is documented as a required step in the change process.
levelDescriptions.4: Impact analysis is evidenced in change records and consumers are notified before release.
levelDescriptions.5: Impact analysis is automated in the deployment pipeline and blocks changes with unresolved downstream breaks.

questions.text: Are manual interventions — spreadsheets, hand adjustments, end-user computing — in critical data flows identified and risk-rated?

levelDescriptions.1: Unknown. Manual steps are embedded throughout and nobody has inventoried them.
levelDescriptions.2: The main spreadsheets are known informally to the teams that operate them.
levelDescriptions.3: An inventory of manual interventions in critical flows exists.
levelDescriptions.4: Interventions are risk-rated, controlled, and a reduction backlog is actively worked.
levelDescriptions.5: Critical flows are free of uncontrolled manual intervention; any remaining steps are controlled and evidenced.

questions.text: Can the derivation of a regulatory return line item be evidenced to a regulator on request, end to end?

levelDescriptions.1: Not without a multi-week investigation dependent on specific individuals.
levelDescriptions.2: Partial documentation exists for major returns but is incomplete and dated.
levelDescriptions.3: Line-item to source-field mapping is documented for the priority returns.
levelDescriptions.4: An evidence pack is maintained current and has been used successfully in an examination.
levelDescriptions.5: Evidence is generated on demand from live lineage rather than maintained as a separate document.

questions.text: Is the lineage of anti-money-laundering and transaction-monitoring inputs documented and defensible?

levelDescriptions.1: No documented lineage for monitoring inputs; completeness of feeds is assumed rather than evidenced.
levelDescriptions.2: Feed documentation exists at interface level without field-level traceability.
levelDescriptions.3: Field-level lineage is documented for monitoring and screening inputs.
levelDescriptions.4: Feed completeness is monitored with alerting on gaps, and lineage is maintained through change.
levelDescriptions.5: Completeness and lineage evidence is produced automatically for each reporting period.

questions.text: Is data classified by sensitivity at column level, with the classification recorded in the catalogue?

levelDescriptions.1: No classification. Sensitivity is assumed from system context rather than recorded.
levelDescriptions.2: A classification scheme exists on paper but has not been applied to actual data assets.
levelDescriptions.3: Governed elements are classified and the classification is recorded in the catalogue.
levelDescriptions.4: Classification coverage is measured, reviewed periodically, and drives access and masking controls.
levelDescriptions.5: Classification is applied automatically at ingestion with steward validation of exceptions.

questions.text: Are access entitlements approved by the Data Owner and recertified on a defined cycle?

levelDescriptions.1: Access is granted by IT on request with no business approval and is never reviewed.
levelDescriptions.2: Approval is sought informally from whoever is available; no recertification takes place.
levelDescriptions.3: The Data Owner approves access and a recertification cycle is defined.
levelDescriptions.4: Recertification is executed on cycle with exceptions revoked and evidenced.
levelDescriptions.5: Entitlements are role-derived and drift is detected automatically between recertification cycles.

questions.text: Is sensitive data masked or tokenised in non-production environments?

levelDescriptions.1: Production data is copied to development and test environments unmasked.
levelDescriptions.2: Masking is applied inconsistently, typically only where a specific audit point required it.
levelDescriptions.3: A masking standard exists and is applied to sensitive elements in non-production.
levelDescriptions.4: Masking is enforced in the environment provisioning process and coverage is verified.
levelDescriptions.5: Non-production environments never receive unmasked sensitive data by construction, with automated verification.

questions.text: Can the bank state, per data element, what may be shared with an AI service or third-party processor?

levelDescriptions.1: No. AI and third-party proposals stall because the exposure question cannot be answered.
levelDescriptions.2: Assessed case by case with substantial effort and inconsistent conclusions.
levelDescriptions.3: Classification and sharing rules are documented at element level for governed data.
levelDescriptions.4: A defined intake assesses each use case against classification, with recorded decisions.
levelDescriptions.5: Controls are technically enforced so non-permitted elements cannot reach an external processor.

questions.text: Are customer confidentiality and cross-border processing constraints documented and enforced in the data estate?

levelDescriptions.1: Constraints are known to legal in principle but not reflected in any technical control.
levelDescriptions.2: Documented in policy; enforcement relies on individual awareness.
levelDescriptions.3: Constraints are mapped to specific data elements and systems.
levelDescriptions.4: Technical controls enforce residency and sharing constraints, with exceptions registered.
levelDescriptions.5: Constraint compliance is continuously monitored and evidenced for regulators and auditors.

questions.text: Does a retention schedule exist per data category with a documented legal basis?

levelDescriptions.1: No schedule. Data is retained indefinitely by default.
levelDescriptions.2: Retention periods are mentioned in policy without mapping to actual data categories or systems.
levelDescriptions.3: A schedule exists per category with legal basis recorded and legal sign-off obtained.
levelDescriptions.4: The schedule is applied operationally with archival and disposal actually executed.
levelDescriptions.5: Retention is enforced automatically with evidence of disposal retained for audit.

questions.text: Is the number and purpose of data copies across environments known?

levelDescriptions.1: Unknown. Copies proliferate through project activity with no inventory.
levelDescriptions.2: Major copies are known; extracts and departmental copies are not.
levelDescriptions.3: A copy inventory exists with purpose and owner recorded.
levelDescriptions.4: Redundant copies are identified, attributed to cost, and retired on a worked backlog.
levelDescriptions.5: Copy creation requires registration and justification; the count trends down over time.

questions.text: Is storage cost attributed to the domains that own the data?

levelDescriptions.1: Storage is a central technology cost with no attribution.
levelDescriptions.2: Attribution is estimated occasionally for budget discussions.
levelDescriptions.3: Cost is attributed to owning domains on a documented basis.
levelDescriptions.4: Attributed cost is reported to owners and influences retention decisions.
levelDescriptions.5: Owners actively manage their data footprint against a cost budget.

questions.text: Are statutory record-retention obligations for account, transaction and KYC records mapped to actual system behaviour?

levelDescriptions.1: Obligations are known in principle; no mapping to system retention configuration exists.
levelDescriptions.2: Mapping exists for core banking only, with archives and warehouses unassessed.
levelDescriptions.3: Obligations are mapped across the systems holding the relevant records.
levelDescriptions.4: System configuration is verified against obligations and deviations are remediated.
levelDescriptions.5: Compliance is monitored continuously with legal-hold handling integrated.

questions.text: Is there a defined disposition plan for legacy data from decommissioned or migrated core systems?

levelDescriptions.1: Legacy systems are kept running or their data archived indefinitely with no plan.
levelDescriptions.2: A plan is discussed at migration time but not executed after go-live.
levelDescriptions.3: A disposition plan exists covering retention, access and eventual disposal.
levelDescriptions.4: The plan is executed with evidence, and legacy access is controlled and time-limited.
levelDescriptions.5: Legacy disposition is a standard, repeatable component of every migration programme.

questions.text: Is a data catalogue deployed, integrated with source systems, and actively used outside the governance team?

levelDescriptions.1: No catalogue is deployed.
levelDescriptions.2: A catalogue exists at low coverage and is used almost exclusively by the team that installed it.
levelDescriptions.3: The catalogue is deployed, integrated with the main systems, and coverage is measured.
levelDescriptions.4: Adoption is measured by active users outside the governance team and is growing.
levelDescriptions.5: The catalogue is the default starting point for analysts and engineers seeking data.

questions.text: Are governance policies enforced as code within pipelines, rather than only published as documents?

levelDescriptions.1: No enforcement. Policies exist as documents and compliance is voluntary.
levelDescriptions.2: One or two checks exist in isolated pipelines, built by individual engineers.
levelDescriptions.3: Defined policies have named enforcement points implemented in pipelines or gates.
levelDescriptions.4: Enforcement is standard for new pipelines and failures block promotion to production.
levelDescriptions.5: Policy-as-code is version-controlled, tested and applied estate-wide with exception registration.

questions.text: Is metadata harvesting automated and monitored, with failures alerted?

levelDescriptions.1: Metadata is entered manually or not at all.
levelDescriptions.2: Harvesting runs for some systems but failures go unnoticed until content is found stale.
levelDescriptions.3: Scheduled harvesting is configured with monitoring in place.
levelDescriptions.4: Failures alert to a named owner and freshness is reported as a metric.
levelDescriptions.5: Harvesting is self-healing with freshness maintained within a defined tolerance.

questions.text: Can metadata and lineage be extracted from the vendor core banking platform, or is that estate opaque to governance tooling?

levelDescriptions.1: The core is entirely opaque; no metadata extraction has been attempted.
levelDescriptions.2: Extraction is manual, via documentation or one-off vendor requests.
levelDescriptions.3: A documented extraction approach exists and has been proven for the core.
levelDescriptions.4: Core metadata is harvested on schedule into the catalogue.
levelDescriptions.5: Core lineage is captured to field level and maintained automatically through vendor releases.

questions.text: Is governance tooling integrated with the bank's existing change and release management process?

levelDescriptions.1: No integration. Governance activity runs outside the bank's change process entirely.
levelDescriptions.2: Governance raises change requests manually where someone remembers to.
levelDescriptions.3: Governance steps are defined within the standard change process.
levelDescriptions.4: Change records reference catalogue and lineage impact analysis as a required input.
levelDescriptions.5: Change approval is automatically gated on governance checks passing.

questions.text: Is there a register of certified reports and trusted datasets that consumers are directed to use?

levelDescriptions.1: No register. Consumers build their own extracts and reports independently.
levelDescriptions.2: Some reports are informally regarded as authoritative without formal certification.
levelDescriptions.3: A certification standard exists and a register of certified assets is published.
levelDescriptions.4: Certified assets carry owners and quality measures, and uncertified proliferation is being reduced.
levelDescriptions.5: Certification status is surfaced in consumption tools at the point of use.

questions.text: Do AI and analytics use cases pass a data-readiness gate before development is approved?

levelDescriptions.1: No gate. Use cases start and later discover the data cannot support them.
levelDescriptions.2: Data suitability is considered informally by the delivery team.
levelDescriptions.3: A documented readiness assessment is required at intake.
levelDescriptions.4: The gate is enforced — use cases failing it do not proceed until gaps are closed.
levelDescriptions.5: Readiness is assessed automatically from catalogue, classification and quality metadata.

questions.text: Are model and analytics inputs traceable to governed data elements?

levelDescriptions.1: No traceability. Inputs are assembled by the modelling team from whatever sources they locate.
levelDescriptions.2: Inputs are documented at dataset level without element-level traceability.
levelDescriptions.3: Inputs are traced to governed elements and recorded in model documentation.
levelDescriptions.4: Input quality metrics are reported alongside model performance.
levelDescriptions.5: Model drift is attributable to input data change, and input changes notify model owners automatically.

questions.text: Is the content used to ground generative AI — documents, policies, customer records — classified and access-controlled before ingestion?

levelDescriptions.1: No control. Either nothing is deployed, or content is ingested without classification review.
levelDescriptions.2: Reviewed manually per pilot with inconsistent criteria.
levelDescriptions.3: A classification and approval process governs what may be ingested.
levelDescriptions.4: Access controls on the source are preserved through to the AI consumption layer.
levelDescriptions.5: Ingestion is automatically gated on classification, with entitlement enforced at query time.

questions.text: Does model risk management require evidenced data lineage for regulatory and credit models?

levelDescriptions.1: Data lineage is not part of model validation.
levelDescriptions.2: Validation notes data sources at a high level without lineage evidence.
levelDescriptions.3: Lineage evidence is a documented requirement of model validation.
levelDescriptions.4: Validation is blocked where lineage evidence is absent, and this is enforced in practice.
levelDescriptions.5: Lineage evidence is produced automatically from the governance platform for each validation cycle.
